AI Foundations · Lesson 7 · 30 minutes

Learning with no answers

Clustering, PCA and anomaly detection: finding structure nobody labelled.

Press N for presenter lines · F fullscreen · arrows to move

No answer column. Three useful jobs.

Group

Clustering: which customers are alike? (marketing segments)

Compress

Dimensionality reduction: 34 columns → a few that keep most information

Spot oddities

Anomaly detection: which records look nothing like the rest? (fraud, broken data)

Why? Labels are expensive: someone has to wait months to see who churns, or pay experts to tag data. Unlabelled data is almost free and almost endless. Modern LLMs learned mostly from unlabelled text.

Part A · Clustering

k-means in four steps

1 Choose k, the number of groups; drop k centres among the customers
2 Assign every customer to the nearest centre
3 Move each centre to the average of its customers
4 Repeat 2–3 until nothing moves
Why? Each round lowers the total squared distance from customers to their centre, so it always settles. But it settles in the nearest valley, not necessarily the best one (like greedy trees in Lesson 5).

"Nearest" means distance, and distance has units

Forget to scale and one column decides everything

Why? In raw dollars, TotalCharges holds 99.97% of all the spread (thousands of $ vs tens of months), so k-means just slices by total bill. Scale first (Lesson 4): every feature gets a fair vote.

How many groups? Two tests on our data

Why? Clustering on tenure, monthly bill and number of services (scaled). Elbow: adding groups always lowers distance; look for the bend. Silhouette: for each customer, how much closer to its own group than the next one (−1 to 1). Both point to k = 4.

Choosing k: all the options

MethodIdeaOn our dataCatch
Elbowwhere extra groups stop helping muchbend at ~4the bend is often vague
Silhouetteseparation of groupsbest k = 4 (0.427)favours round, equal blobs
BIC (Gaussian mixture)fit vs complexity scorekeeps falling to k = 9chases details: "services" has only 10 values
Stabilitydo groups survive resampling?k = 4 stable (see later)costs extra runs
Business sensecan a team act on each group?4 nameable segmentssubjective, but decisive
Best choice: shortlist k with silhouette + elbow, then pick the k whose groups the business can name and act on. There is no "true" k in real data.

The 4 segments k-means found

Why? k-means never saw the churn column. Yet its groups range from 4% to 47% churn. Structure found without answers turned out to matter for the answer.

From clusters to actions

SegmentCustomersProfileChurnAction
New, high bill2,41215 months · $77 · 86% month-to-month47%contract upgrade offer, early check-in
New, budget1,50310 months · $29 · few services24%onboarding, bundle trial
Loyal, premium2,15657 months · $91 · 6.7 services16%protect: loyalty perks
Loyal, basic97254 months · $30 · 2 services4%gentle upsell

Run it twice, get different groups?

SettingAgreement between 10 runs with different random starts (ARI)
n_init = 1 (one start)worst 0.51 · average 0.89
n_init = 10 (best of 10 starts)worst 0.996
Why? ARI = 1 means identical groupings, 0 means random. A single start can land in a poor valley. Running 10 starts and keeping the lowest-distance one makes the result repeatable. Smart starting points (k-means++, the default) help too.
Best choice: k-means++ with n_init ≥ 10, and a fixed random_state so reports are reproducible.

k-means' blind spot: it only sees round blobs

Why? k-means splits space into straight-edged regions around centres. Two curved moons defeat it (ARI 0.25). DBSCAN grows groups from dense neighbourhoods, follows any shape, and labels lonely points as noise (ARI 1.0).

Five clustering algorithms on our churn data

AlgorithmIdeaGroupsSilhouetteChurn spreadBest for
k-meansnearest centre40.4343 ptssegments, big data, speed
Gaussian mixturesoft, oval groups with probabilities40.3136 ptswhen a customer can be "60% A, 40% B"
Hierarchical (Ward)merge closest groups step by step40.3844 ptssmall data; a family-tree view
DBSCANdense regions, any shape170.1160 ptsodd shapes, spatial data
HDBSCANDBSCAN without the eps guess13 + 32% noise0.2165 ptsunknown k, noisy data
Best choice: k-means for customer segmentation (clear, fast, actionable); HDBSCAN when groups have odd shapes or you can't guess k; Gaussian mixtures when you need soft membership.

Two honest warnings

Clusters are a lens, not a fact

Silhouette 0.43 means the groups touch. Customers form a continuous cloud; k-means will always return k groups, even from pure noise.

Segments didn't help prediction

Adding the segment to our logistic model: CV AUC 0.8451 → 0.8456. The model already had the raw features the segments came from.

Why? Use clustering to understand and communicate; don't expect it to boost a supervised model that already sees the same columns.

Part B · Compress: PCA

34 columns, but far fewer independent ideas

1 "No internet service" appears in 7 different columns: they all say the same thing
2 PCA finds new directions (components) along which customers spread out the most
3 Keep the top few; drop directions with little spread
Why? Like photographing a 3-D object from the angle that shows the most: you lose one dimension but keep the recognisable shape.

How many components do we need?

Why? The first component alone holds 30% of the information. 15 components keep 90%; 18 keep 95%. Roughly half the columns carry almost everything.

What do the components mean? Read the weights

PC1 (30%): "internet & extras"

+ "no internet service" columns (0.30 each)
− monthly bill (−0.28), streaming, fiber

PC2 (13%): "loyalty"

+ tenure (0.41), total charges, two-year contract
− month-to-month (−0.40), electronic check

Why? Nobody told PCA about "loyalty". It discovered that tenure, contract type and payment method move together, because that is how customers really behave.

Seeing 34 dimensions on a flat screen

Why? Leavers (red) sit on the low-loyalty side of PCA's map. t-SNE makes tighter islands of similar customers, but only for viewing: distances between islands and island sizes mean nothing, and it can't map new customers.

Does compressing help the churn model?

Why? 2 components already reach 0.813; 12 reach 0.843; but using all 34 columns is still best (0.845). PCA chooses directions by spread, not by usefulness for churn, and our regularised model already copes with redundancy.

Reducing dimensions: all the options

MethodKeepsUse forCatch
PCAlargest straight-line spreadcompression, speed, de-noising, quick mapsonly straight-line structure; scale first
t-SNElocal neighbourspictures of clustersslow; distances misleading; no new points
UMAPneighbours + some global shapefaster, better maps; can map new pointsstill mainly for viewing; tune neighbours
Autoencoder (neural net)any curved structureimages, huge dataneeds Part II skills and lots of data
Feature selection (Lasso, Lesson 4)original, readable columnssimpler models people can readuses the label (supervised)
Best choice: PCA first for compression and a quick look; UMAP for pictures; and if the goal is prediction, prefer regularisation or feature selection over PCA.

Part C · Spot oddities

Isolation forest: weird points are easy to isolate

1 Cut the data with random splits (random feature, random value)
2 A normal customer sits in a crowd: it takes many cuts to isolate it
3 An odd customer is alone: a few cuts isolate it → high anomaly score
Why? Experiment: we secretly corrupted 35 of 7,043 bills (TotalCharges × 5–12). Flag the top 1% (70 customers) as suspicious:

Which corrupted bills did it catch?

Input to isolation forestCorrupted bills caught in top 1%
tenure, monthly, total (raw columns)29 / 35
+ one domain feature: total ÷ (months × monthly)35 / 35
Why? A correct bill has total ≈ months × monthly, so the ratio ≈ 1. Corrupted bills have ratio 5–12. One feature built from business knowledge beat any algorithm tweak.
Best choice: simple rules (ratio checks, z-scores) for known problems; isolation forest for unknown ones; and always give it features that encode what "normal" means. Use it for fraud, sensor faults and broken data pipelines.

Which unsupervised tool, when?

GoalReach for
Customer / product segmentsscaled features → k-means (n_init ≥ 10) → name the groups
Groups of odd shape, unknown numberHDBSCAN
Too many columns; speed up; de-noisePCA (keep 90–95% variance)
A picture of high-dimensional dataUMAP or t-SNE (view only)
Fraud, broken records, sensor faultsdomain rules + isolation forest
Better churn predictionprobably not these: supervised models already see the columns

Say this in an interview

1 "How do you choose k?" → silhouette + elbow to shortlist, then stability and whether the business can act on each group; there is no true k
2 "Why scale before k-means or PCA?" → both use distance or variance; unscaled, the biggest-unit column (TotalCharges: 99.97% of spread) dominates
3 "PCA vs t-SNE?" → PCA: linear, fast, reusable on new data; t-SNE: non-linear, for viewing only, distances between clusters are meaningless

Bridge to modern AI

Unsupervised ideas power LLMs and RAG

1 Embeddings: an LLM turns any text into a list of numbers, a learned "PCA" of meaning; similar texts land close together
2 Vector databases (for RAG) often run k-means on millions of embeddings to group them, so search checks only the nearest groups
3 Pre-training: LLMs learn from unlabelled text by predicting the next word; no human answers needed

Check yourself · 1 of 5

You run k-means on raw tenure, monthly bill and total charges. What goes wrong?

AnswerTotalCharges (thousands of $) dominates distance, 99.97% of the spread, so groups just slice by total bill. Scale first.

Check yourself · 2 of 5

Silhouette: 0.42 at k=2, 0.43 at k=4, 0.37 at k=7. Which k, and what else would you check?

Answerk = 4 is a fair shortlist; then check stability and whether each group is actionable for the business.

Check yourself · 3 of 5

Your data has two curved, interlocking groups. k-means or DBSCAN?

AnswerDBSCAN (or HDBSCAN): it follows dense regions of any shape; k-means assumes round blobs.

Check yourself · 4 of 5

PCA keeps 95% of variance with 18 of 34 columns. Will your churn model get more accurate?

AnswerNot necessarily. PCA keeps spread, not churn signal. Ours: 0.843 with PCA vs 0.845 without.

Check yourself · 5 of 5

A colleague shows a t-SNE plot: "these two islands are far apart, so they're very different." Right?

AnswerNo. t-SNE keeps neighbours, not long distances; gaps and island sizes aren't meaningful.
RememberScale first. Group with k-means, compress with PCA,
flag oddities with isolation forest.
Structure is a lens: name it, test it, act on it.
